items.title: Cells make energy by pumping ACID uphill
items.claim: Mitochondria spend most of their energy budget pumping protons across the inner membrane against a steep electrochemical gradient. Only after building this acidic outer space do they let the protons flow back through ATP synthase, capturing the energy.
items.prompt: Why not just make ATP directly during electron transport?

options.text: Chemiosmosis lets the cell decouple ENERGY EXTRACTION (electron transport) from ENERGY USE (ATP synthesis); the proton gradient is a rechargeable battery that links any electron donor to any ATP demand
The gradient is a side-effect with no function

items.reveal_title: Mitchell's chemiosmotic hypothesis — initially dismissed, then Nobel-winning
items.reveal:
Peter Mitchell proposed in 1961 that ATP synthesis was driven by a proton gradient, not by direct chemistry. Biochemists hated the idea — it seemed to require a 'metabolic battery' instead of a chemical intermediate. Mitchell was right, and won the 1978 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

The inner mitochondrial membrane is impermeable to protons. Electrons flowing through the respiratory chain pump protons OUT, building a pH gradient (~ 0.7 units) and an electric potential (~ 150 mV) — together about 200 mV of proton motive force.

ATP synthase is essentially a rotary motor turned by proton flow. The number of protons per ATP is fractional (about 3.7 to 4) because synthase geometry doesn't match the chemistry of ATP cleanly.
items.why: Energy currency feels like chemistry. Living cells use a physical gradient — a battery — as the actual unit of energy transfer.

items.title: Lions get only 0.001% of the sun's energy that hit their grass
items.claim: Each trophic level passes about 10% of its energy to the next. Sun -> grass -> antelope -> lion. Three steps means lions retain 0.1% of grass energy. Add another step and you're down to 0.01%. The tenth-of-energy rule explains why food chains are short.

options.text: Most of the consumed energy goes to respiration (powering the consumer's metabolism), heat loss, and undigested waste; only a small fraction is converted into new tissue available to the next predator

items.reveal:
Raymond Lindeman (1942) measured energy flow in Cedar Bog Lake, Minnesota. He found progressive losses at each trophic level — formalising 'trophic efficiency'.

Typical values: primary producers fix ~1-2% of incident solar energy as net primary productivity. Herbivores extract ~10% of plant productivity. Carnivores ~10% of herbivore productivity. Top predators get a tiny fraction of the original solar input.

Consequences: food chains rarely exceed 4-5 trophic levels; predators have huge home ranges and small populations; ecosystems with apex predators are inherently fragile to disruption at the base.

The '10% rule' is an approximation. Efficiencies actually vary: ectotherms (fish, reptiles) can transfer 30-40% because they don't spend energy maintaining body heat. Endotherms (mammals, birds) burn most of what they eat to stay warm.

Vegetarian arguments often invoke this: feeding plants directly to people is ~10x more energy-efficient than routing them through livestock first.
items.why: Food chains feel boundless. Thermodynamics caps them at 4 or 5 links. Each predator carries the entropic cost of every prey it ate.

items.title: The oxygen you breathe comes from WATER, not CO2
items.claim: Photosynthesis takes in CO2 and water and produces sugar and oxygen. Every chemistry student writes the equation. But the O2 released is not stripped from the CO2 — it comes entirely from splitting water molecules.
items.prompt: How do we know the oxygen comes from water?

options.text: Both water and CO2 contribute oxygen equally
Ruben and Kamen (1941) used the heavy isotope oxygen-18 to label either water or CO2; the released O2 carried the label only when the water was labelled, never when the CO2 was
CO2 is the source of the oxygen

items.reveal:
The light reactions of photosynthesis split water (photolysis) at the oxygen-evolving complex — a manganese-calcium cluster in Photosystem II. Two water molecules are split: 2 H2O -> 4 H+ + 4 e- + O2.

The electrons enter the electron transport chain. The protons contribute to the thylakoid pH gradient (lumen reaches pH ~5, stroma ~8). ATP synthase uses the gradient to make ATP.

The Calvin cycle (in the stroma) uses ATP and NADPH to fix CO2 into sugar. The carbon from CO2 becomes the carbon in glucose. But the oxygen atoms in CO2 mostly end up in carbohydrate, NOT in the released O2.

Oxygen is, from photosynthesis's point of view, a waste product — and arguably the most consequential pollution event in Earth's history (the Great Oxidation Event, ~2.4 billion years ago, killed most anaerobic life).
items.why: The arrow-pushing equation suggests CO2 donates oxygen. The actual chemistry inverts that: water is split, CO2 is reduced, and the oxygen you breathe was once dissolved in a chloroplast.
